    structure CoreCpp.Binding : Type
    structure CoreCpp.Binding : Type
    A binding of ρ. `owned` records whether the declaration that created the
binding allocated the location, as `τ x = e` does, or aliased an existing one,
as the reference `τ& y = e` does. Block exit frees only owned locations, so an
alias never removes the location of the variable it names.

    Fields

    loc : CoreCpp.Loc
    The location the identifier denotes. 
    owned : Bool
    Whether the declaration allocated the location, so scope exit frees it.

    Top level declarations. A `tmpl T C` is a class template, the class `C`

    inductive CoreCpp.Error : Type
    inductive CoreCpp.Error : Type
    The `error` result of the evaluator. It is not a value of the language. No
syntax produces, tests or catches it. It corresponds in C++ to abnormal
program termination. The relations of `CoreCpp.Semantics` have no `error`,
and the evaluator gives one where no rule has a derivation. The causes
`undeclaredVariable`, `undeclaredFunction`, `arity`, `typeError` and
`notCallable` guard the evaluator against a program that skipped the type
checker, and `outOfFuel` marks a derivation deeper than the fuel.

    def CoreCpp.Eval.applyClosure (fuel : Nat) (fs : CoreCpp.FunEnv)
  (ρ : CoreCpp.Env) (σ : CoreCpp.Store) (v : CoreCpp.Val)
  (es : List CoreCpp.Expr) : CoreCpp.M (CoreCpp.Val × CoreCpp.Store)
    def CoreCpp.Eval.applyClosure (fuel : Nat)
  (fs : CoreCpp.FunEnv) (ρ : CoreCpp.Env)
  (σ : CoreCpp.Store) (v : CoreCpp.Val)
  (es : List CoreCpp.Expr) :
  CoreCpp.M (CoreCpp.Val × CoreCpp.Store)
    The application of a closure to arguments.

```
v = closure(x₁ … xₖ, τ, c, [y₁ ↦ w₁, …, yₘ ↦ wₘ])
the arguments as in `args`, values v₁ … vₖ, store σₖ
(ℓ'ⱼ, ·) = alloc wⱼ    (ℓᵢ, ·) = alloc vᵢ
ρ_c = [y₁ ↦ ℓ'₁, …, yₘ ↦ ℓ'ₘ, x₁ ↦ ℓ₁, …, xₖ ↦ ℓₖ]
ρ_c, σ' ⊢ c ⇒ ret r, ρ'', σ''    rd(σ'', r) = v
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (Apply)
apply v (e₁, …, eₖ) ⇒ v, σ'' ∖ ({ℓ'ⱼ, ℓᵢ} ∪ (ρ'' ∖ ρ_c))
```

The arguments evaluate left to right, by value. The locations ℓ'ⱼ and ℓᵢ are
fresh, for the copies and for the parameters. The environment ρ_c holds the
closure environment and nothing else is visible. On the way out the copies,
the parameters and the locals leave the store.

With normal in place of ret r the result is void if τ = void and error
(missing return) otherwise. A value that is not a closure is error.

    def CoreCpp.Eval.binop :
  CoreCpp.BinOp → CoreCpp.Val → CoreCpp.Val → CoreCpp.M CoreCpp.Val
    def CoreCpp.Eval.binop :
  CoreCpp.BinOp →
    CoreCpp.Val →
      CoreCpp.Val → CoreCpp.M CoreCpp.Val
    Arithmetic and relational binary operators, on already evaluated values.

```
ρ, σ ⊢ e₁ ⇒ int n₁, σ₁    ρ, σ₁ ⊢ e₂ ⇒ int n₂, σ₂
──────────────────────────────────────────────── (Arith, ⊕ ∈ {+, -, *})
ρ, σ ⊢ e₁ ⊕ e₂ ⇒ int32 (n₁ ⊕ n₂), σ₂
```

```
ρ, σ ⊢ e₁ ⇒ int n₁, σ₁    ρ, σ₁ ⊢ e₂ ⇒ int n₂, σ₂    n₂ ≠ 0
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── (Div, ⊘ ∈ {/, %})
ρ, σ ⊢ e₁ ⊘ e₂ ⇒ int32 (n₁ ⊘ n₂), σ₂          division truncates toward zero, as in C++
```

A zero divisor and a result outside the range of `int` have no derivation,
and `binop` gives `error` for them. The quotient of −2³¹ by −1 is such a
result, while the remainder of −2³¹ by −1 is 0.

```
ρ, σ ⊢ e₁ ⇒ v₁, σ₁    ρ, σ₁ ⊢ e₂ ⇒ v₂, σ₂
─────────────────────────────────────────── (Rel, ⋈ ∈ {==, !=, <, <=, >, >=})
ρ, σ ⊢ e₁ ⋈ e₂ ⇒ bool (v₁ ⋈ v₂), σ₂
```

Two pointers are equal when they are the same location. nullptr equals
only nullptr. There is no order on pointers.

The left operand is evaluated before the right one, the Core C++ choice
where C++17 does not specify the order.

    inductive CoreCpp.Expr : Type
    inductive CoreCpp.Expr : Type
    Expressions.

The forms a program writes. `field` is `e.f`, `arrow` is `e->f`, `deref` is
`*e` and `index` is `e[i]`. `newObj C args` is `new C(args)`, which allocates
the object and runs the constructor, and `newLib τ args` is `new τ(args)` for
a type of the library, `new std::vector<int>(3)` for instance. `this` is the
location of the receiver inside a method.

`call f args` calls the function named `f`, or the `std::function` that a
reference `f` in scope names, or the method `f` of `this` inside a class.
`callFn e args` calls the `std::function` that `e` denotes, as in `(*f)(ē)`.
Function call is a form of `Expr` because `Args` is part of `PostfixExpr`.

`methodCall e arrow m args static sig` is `e.m(args)` when `arrow` is false
and `e->m(args)` when it is true. `lambda ps τ c` is `[=](ps) -> τ { c }`,
which the grammar admits only as an argument of `new`, and the type checker
only as the argument of `new std::function<F>(λ)`.

Two fields carry what the type checker learns and the evaluator needs. The
field `static` of `methodCall` is the class of the receiver as the type
checker sees it, which tells a dispatched call from a static one.

The field `sig` of `call` and of `methodCall` is the parameter type list of
the overload it chose, which picks one function or method out of an overload
set. Both fields are `none` as the parser leaves them, and `Typing.annotate`
fills them.

    Whether the method is virtual, declared `virtual` or marked `override`.
A method that overrides a virtual method is virtual whether or not it is
declared `virtual` (N4659 §13.3 paragraph 2), and `override` marks exactly
the methods that override one, by the rule T-Class. So a call through a
pointer to a middle class of a chain dispatches, and a third class may
override the method again.

and repeat no field of a base. The members have distinct names, and each
method redefines only a method the base declares `virtual`, carrying
`override` and the same signature. The constructor of the base, if the base
has one, takes no parameters. Every member body is well typed under `this`.

          | "->" VarId After | Args Chain ) ] ;

ChainNoCall = [ ( "[" Expr "]" Chain | "." VarId After
                | "->" VarId After ) ] ;

any other postfix expression it is the call of the `std::function` that
expression denotes, `callFn`, as in `(*f)(ē)`. The forms `.m(…)`
and `->m(…)` are method calls, with the static class left for the type checker, and

    The nonrecursive predictive parser. The stack starts with the start symbol.
A terminal on top must match the next token, and the parser pops it and
consumes the token. For a nonterminal `A` on top, the table gives a production
for `A` and the lookahead, the first one when the entry holds several. The
parser replaces `A` by the right side of that production and outputs its
index. The parser accepts when stack and input end together, and its output
is the leftmost derivation. It runs within a fuel bound and fails with

nonterminals can exhaust it on a valid input.

Neither \rho nor \sigma carries types, and the rules MethodCall and Delete need the static class of the receiver.

After a program is checked, annotate walks it with the typing context. It writes into every method call and every delete the class the receiver has in \Gamma. It also rewrites an unqualified m(args) inside a member body into this->m(args).

A program runs only when it parses, type checks and annotates. The function prepare checks the program and annotates it. A program that check rejects stops with its type error. A failure of annotate on a program that check accepts is an error of the implementation, and the program stops too.

A class has an optional base, fields and methods with a visibility, at most one constructor named after the class and at most one destructor. Members before the first section label are private, as in C++ (N4659 §14 paragraph 3).

The class is well formed, \vdash C, when the conditions of ClassOk hold. The base exists and the chain of bases is acyclic. The fields have distinct names, repeat no field of a base, and have storable, non void and well formed types. No method has the name of a field. Two methods of one name are distinguishable, Definition 7.1.1, and no signature occurs twice. An operator member takes one parameter, Definition 7.2.1.

A method that redefines a method of a base finds it virtual there, carries override and keeps the signature, and override marks only a redefinition. The result types are void or storable, the parameter types bindable, and all are well formed. The constructor of the base takes no parameters, since there are no initialiser lists. Every member body is well typed under this, and a member that returns a reference satisfies T-RetRef of Definition 7.2.2.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} B \text{ exists, chain acyclic}\qquad \text{fields distinct, new in the chain, storable, not void, well formed} \\ \text{no method named as a field}\qquad \text{methods of one name distinguishable, no signature twice}\qquad \text{operators with one parameter} \\ \text{each redefined } m \text{ is virtual in the base, marked override, same signature}\qquad \text{override only on a redefinition} \\ \text{results void or storable, parameters bindable, all well formed}\qquad B \text{ has no constructor or one without parameters} \\ [\mathtt{this} \mapsto C*, p_1, \ldots, p_k] \vdash c \dashv \Gamma' \text{ with its result type, for each member body}\qquad \text{T-RetRef for each member returning } \tau\& \end{array}}{\vdash \mathtt{class}\ C\ \mathtt{:}\ \mathtt{public}\ B\ \{ \ldots \}}\;\textsf{(T-Class)}

The context of a member body binds this to C* and the parameters as variables, so the current class is the class of this in \Gamma.

The command delete e applies to a pointer to a class or to an object type of the library, whose rule DeleteLib in Definition 8.1.2 frees what the module owns and then the location of the instance.

On an object it runs the destructors of the chain from the tag up to the root, each with this bound to the object, and removes the record and the field locations from \sigma.

A second delete and any later access through the pointer have no derivation. So does a delete through a pointer to a base without a virtual destructor in its chain. The evaluator gives error in the three cases, which C++17 leaves undefined (N4659 §8.3.5 paragraphs 2 and 3, §6.7 paragraph 4). The command delete nullptr runs no destructor, as in C++ (N4659 §8.3.5 paragraph 6).

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : C*}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{delete}\ e \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-Delete)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : L\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle* \qquad L\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle \text{ an object type} \qquad \Gamma \vdash_L \mathtt{delete}\ \mathsf{ok}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{delete}\ e \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-DeleteLib)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma_0 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_0, r) = \mathsf{loc}\,\ell\qquad \sigma_0(\ell) = \mathsf{obj}\,T\,[f_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, f_n \mapsto \ell_n] \\ S \text{ the static class of } e\qquad S = T \text{ or the chain of } S \text{ has a virtual destructor} \\ \text{the destructors of the chain of } T \text{ run from } T \text{ up, giving } \sigma_1 \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{delete}\ e \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma_1 \setminus \{\ell, \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_n\}}\;\textsf{(Delete)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma_0 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_0, r) = \mathsf{null}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{delete}\ e \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma_0}\;\textsf{(DeleteNull)}

A method is virtual when it is declared virtual or marked override, Method.virtual. An override is virtual without the word virtual, as in C++ (N4659 §13.3 paragraph 2). A third class of a chain may therefore override it again, and a call through a pointer to the middle class dispatches.

The class tag T of the receiver chooses a virtual method, the nearest declaration in the chain of T, so a call through a base pointer reaches the override of the derived class. The static class S chooses a non virtual method.

A derived class redefines only a method that is virtual in the base, and marks it override. So the method reached from S and the one reached from T coincide for every non virtual method.

Redefining a non virtual method, marking override without a virtual method in a base, or changing the signature is a type error.

For every well typed program, the method a call resolves to by the static class of the receiver and the method it resolves to by the class tag coincide whenever the method is not virtual.

The nearest declaration of a non virtual m from S is also the nearest from T, because no class between T and S redeclares m with its signature. The property follows from the rule T-Class by inspection, and there is no Lean proof.

The call of a member body, a method, a constructor or a destructor, binds this to the location \ell of the receiver as an alias. It binds the parameters as the call of a function does, by value with a fresh copy and by reference with an alias. The return frees the copies and the locals of the body, never the receiver.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \text{for each } i \text{ left to right, } \sigma'_0 = \sigma \\ p_i = \tau_i \colon \ \rho, \sigma'_{i-1} \vdash e_i \Rightarrow r_i, \sigma_i \quad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_i, r_i) = v_i \quad (\ell_i, \sigma'_i) = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma_i, v_i) \\ p_i = \tau_i\& \colon \ \rho, \sigma'_{i-1} \vdash e_i \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell_i, \sigma'_i \\ \rho_m = [\mathtt{this} \mapsto \ell, x_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, x_k \mapsto \ell_k]\qquad \rho_m, \sigma'_k \vdash c \Rightarrow \kappa, \rho', \sigma'' \qquad \mathsf{Returns}(\sigma'', \kappa, \tau, r) \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathrm{member}\ \ell\ (e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow r, \sigma'' \setminus (\{\ell_i \mid p_i \text{ by value}\} \cup \mathrm{fresh}(\rho_m, \rho'))}\;\textsf{(Member)}

The predicate \mathsf{Returns} of Definition 5.1.1 gives the result, read before the locals leave the store, or for a member declared \tau\& the location the operand of return yields, rule Returns-Ref of Definition 7.2.2. A non void member that ends without return has no derivation, an error of the evaluator.

A method call e.m(args) needs a receiver of class type and e->m(args) a receiver of pointer type. The method is the nearest m in the chain of the static class of the receiver, it must be visible, and the arguments are checked as in a call. An unqualified call m(args) inside a member body is this->m(args). The result is a value for a method declared \tau and a location for a method declared \tau\&, Definition 7.2.2. One rule covers both, since the member gives the result its declaration prescribes.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash e : C\qquad C \text{ has } \tau\ m(p_1\,x_1, \ldots, p_k\,x_k) \text{ visible from } \Gamma \\ \text{arguments as in T-Call} \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash e.m(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Method)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash e : C*\qquad C \text{ has } \tau\ m(\ldots) \text{ visible from } \Gamma \\ \text{arguments as in T-Call} \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash e\mathtt{->}m(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-MethodArrow)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, \sigma_0 \text{ for } e.m \text{, or } \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_0, \sigma_0 \text{ and } \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_0, r_0) = \mathsf{loc}\,\ell \text{ for } e\mathtt{->}m \\ \sigma_0(\ell) = \mathsf{obj}\,T\,[\ldots] \qquad S \text{ the static class of } e \\ m \mapsto \tau\ m(\ldots)\{c\} \text{ nearest } S \text{, or nearest } T \text{ when virtual} \\ \rho, \sigma_0 \vdash \mathrm{member}\ \ell\ (e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow r, \sigma' \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e.m(e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow r, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(MethodCall)}

A namespace N { … } holds classes, class templates and namespaces, and the parser flattens it. Every class and class template declared inside is named N::C, and the parser reads every unqualified class name in a type or in new inside the namespace as N::C. The type parameter of a class template is the exception. Its name belongs to the template declaration, not to the namespace (N4659 §6.3.9 ¶2), so T inside namespace N { template<typename T> class C { … }; } stays T. Outside the namespace the class has its qualified name, N::C, in types and in new. Namespaces add no rule of typing or of evaluation.

The expression new C(args) allocates one location per field of the whole chain of C, the root base first, and then the tagged record. It runs the constructors from the root base down, each with this bound to the object. The constructor of C receives the arguments and the others none, since there are no initialiser lists.

A class without a constructor is created by new C() and keeps the default values.

\dfrac{C \mapsto \mathtt{class}\ C\ \{\ldots C(p_1\,x_1, \ldots, p_k\,x_k)\ \{c\} \ldots\} \qquad \text{arguments as in T-Call}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{new}\ C(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : C*}\;\textsf{(T-New)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} f_1 \ldots f_n \text{ the fields of the chain of } C\qquad (\ell_i, \sigma_i) = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma_{i-1}, \mathrm{default}\,\tau_i) \\ (\ell, \sigma') = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma_n, \mathsf{obj}\,C\,[f_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, f_n \mapsto \ell_n]) \\ \text{the constructors of the chain run from the root down} \\ \text{with } \mathtt{this} \mapsto \ell \text{, giving } \sigma'' \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{new}\ C(e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{loc}\,\ell), \sigma''}\;\textsf{(New)}

A pointer to a derived class is accepted where a pointer to its base is expected, in declarations, assignments, arguments, returns, comparisons and the branches of ?:. It is the only conversion between pointers to classes, and the other direction is a type error.

\dfrac{D \text{ derives from } B}{\mathsf{Compat}(D*, B*)}\;\textsf{(Subsumption)}

Inside a member body this is the location of the receiver. The call binds it in \rho as an alias, never as a variable, and it evaluates to a pointer. An unqualified name that is not a variable denotes the member of this, both in the type checker and in the evaluator.

\dfrac{\Gamma(\mathtt{this}) = C*}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{this} : C*}\;\textsf{(T-This)}

\dfrac{x \notin \Gamma \qquad \Gamma(\mathtt{this}) = C* \qquad \Gamma \vdash \mathtt{this}\mathtt{->}x : \tau}{\Gamma \vdash x : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-VarField)}

\dfrac{x \notin \Gamma \qquad \Gamma(\mathtt{this}) = C* \qquad \Gamma \vdash_{\ell} \mathtt{this}\mathtt{->}x : \tau}{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} x : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-LocVarField)}

The same holds of a call. An unqualified name that is neither a variable nor a function of the program is a member of the receiver. The evaluator also requires that no header declares the name. The annotation of Definition 6.4.1 rewrites such a call into this->f(…), so CallThis applies only when the evaluator receives a program that was not annotated, which run never passes it.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} f \notin \Gamma\qquad f \text{ is no function of the program}\qquad \Gamma(\mathtt{this}) = C* \\ \Gamma \vdash \mathtt{this}\mathtt{->}f(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : \tau \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash f(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-CallThis)}

\dfrac{\rho(\mathtt{this}) = \ell}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{this} \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{loc}\,\ell), \sigma}\;\textsf{(This)}

\dfrac{x \notin \rho \qquad \rho(\mathtt{this}) = \ell \qquad \sigma(\ell) = \mathsf{obj}\,C\,[\ldots x \mapsto \ell_x \ldots]}{\rho, \sigma \vdash x \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell_x, \sigma}\;\textsf{(VarField)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} f \notin \rho\qquad f \text{ is no function of the program or of a header}\qquad \rho(\mathtt{this}) = \ell \\ \rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{this}\mathtt{->}f(e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow r, \sigma' \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash f(e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow r, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(CallThis)}

A private member declared in class K is visible exactly when \Gamma(\mathtt{this}) = K*. Visibility is thus a typing rule. The public section of a class is the signature of an abstract data type, and the private section is its representation, reachable only from the member bodies of the class.

\dfrac{C \text{ has } \tau\ f \text{ declared in } K \qquad f \text{ public or } \Gamma(\mathtt{this}) = K*}{\Gamma \vdash e.f : \tau \text{ for } \Gamma \vdash e : C}\;\textsf{(Visible)}

The same premise applies to methods, Definition 6.2.3.

The left side denotes a location whose type has values, and the right side has a type with values that \mathsf{Compat} accepts at it, Definition 2.1.11. No assignment writes an object, since an object type has no values. The order is the one C++17 fixes for assignment, the right operand before the left one (N4659 §8.18 paragraph 1). The location must be live, \ell \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma_2, so an assignment through a reference that dangles has no derivation.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e_1 : \tau \qquad \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau) \\ \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \tau' \qquad \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau') \qquad \mathsf{Compat}(\tau', \tau) \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1 = e_2 \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-Assign)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_e) = v \\ \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, \sigma_2 \qquad \ell \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma_2 \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 = e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma_2[\ell \mapsto v]}\;\textsf{(Assign)}

The block discards the extension of \rho and removes from \sigma the locations it allocated. These are the locations \mathrm{fresh}(\rho, \rho') of Definition 2.1.4, so the alias a reference declaration made never frees the location it names. The evaluator computes the same set with Eval.fresh.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash c_1 \ldots c_n \dashv \Gamma'}{\Gamma \vdash \{\, c_1 \ldots c_n \,\} \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-Block)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash c_1 \ldots c_n \Rightarrow r, \rho', \sigma'}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \{\, c_1 \ldots c_n \,\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma' \setminus \mathrm{fresh}(\rho, \rho')}\;\textsf{(Block)}

Every local declaration has an initialiser, by the grammar. The declared type is storable and well formed, the predicate \mathsf{Storable} of Definition 2.1.10 and the judgment \Gamma \vdash \tau\ \mathsf{ok} of Definition 2.1.11. So no variable has an object type, the type \mathsf{nullptr\_t} or a function type. The initialiser is acceptable at the declared type, the judgment \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau of Definition 5.3.1, which requires of the initialiser a type \tau' with values and \mathsf{Compat}(\tau', \tau). A variable of type void therefore has no initialiser that type checks.

With auto, \tau is the type of the initialiser, which has values and is storable.

The declaration evaluates the initialiser, allocates a fresh location with its value, (\ell, \sigma'') = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma', v) of Definition 2.1.5, and extends \rho with the owned binding \rho[x \mapsto \ell], Env.extend, for the following commands. Evaluation ignores the declared type. The relation states the rule Decl twice, the constructor decl for τ x = e and the constructor declAuto for auto x = e.

\dfrac{\mathsf{Storable}(\tau) \qquad \Gamma \vdash \tau\ \mathsf{ok} \qquad \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau}{\Gamma \vdash \tau\ x = e \dashv \Gamma[x \mapsto \tau]}\;\textsf{(T-Decl)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \tau \qquad \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau) \qquad \mathsf{Storable}(\tau)}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{auto}\ x = e \dashv \Gamma[x \mapsto \tau]}\;\textsf{(T-Auto)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma' \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma', r_e) = v \qquad (\ell, \sigma'') = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma', v)}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \tau\ x = e \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho[x \mapsto \ell], \sigma''}\;\textsf{(Decl)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma' \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma', r_e) = v \qquad (\ell, \sigma'') = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma', v)}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{auto}\ x = e \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho[x \mapsto \ell], \sigma''}\;\textsf{(Decl)}

The local reference τ& x = e binds a second name to the location e denotes, without allocating.

The declared type is bindable by reference and well formed, \mathsf{Bindable}_{\mathtt{true}}(\tau) of Definition 2.1.10, so it may be an object type. The initialiser denotes a location of type \tau' with \tau' \sqsubseteq \tau, Typing.refCompat. The relation holds when \tau' = \tau, or when both are classes and \tau' derives from \tau. A reference to a base thus binds an object of a derived class, as in C++ (N4659 §11.6.3 paragraph 5). It never converts a value, so a reference of type int binds only a location of type int. The reference has in \Gamma the declared type \tau, and a call of a virtual method through it dispatches on the class of the object.

The binding \rho[x \mapsto_{\mathsf{a}} \ell] of Definition 2.1.4 is an alias and not owned, so the exit of the block that declared the reference leaves the location in \sigma.

The referent may be an object, as in C& r = *p;, since the reference binds its location and copies nothing. A reference to a temporary, to nullptr or to an expression without a location does not exist. A reference may still dangle. When delete frees an object or a vector, a reference to the object, to one of its fields or to one of its elements names a location outside \sigma. A later read or write through the reference fails a premise \ell \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma, so it has no derivation, and the evaluator gives error with the exit code 134. C++17 leaves that access undefined.

\dfrac{\mathsf{Bindable}_{\mathtt{true}}(\tau) \qquad \Gamma \vdash \tau\ \mathsf{ok} \qquad \Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e : \tau' \qquad \tau' \sqsubseteq \tau}{\Gamma \vdash \tau\mathtt{\&}\ x = e \dashv \Gamma[x \mapsto \tau]}\;\textsf{(T-DeclRef)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, \sigma'}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \tau\mathtt{\&}\ x = e \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho[x \mapsto_{\mathsf{a}} \ell], \sigma'}\;\textsf{(DeclRef)}

An expression followed by ; is a command that evaluates the expression and discards its result, with no conversion (N4659 §8 paragraph 12). The rule accepts any type, void included, so a call to a void function stands as a statement.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \tau}{\Gamma \vdash e; \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-ExprStmt)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma'}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e; \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(ExprStmt)}

The rule For defines for through while. The variable of the initialiser has the loop as its scope, and the loop frees its location at exit, \mathrm{fresh}(\rho, \rho_0) of Definition 4.4.2. The body is a block of its own, and the step runs after the body, outside the body's scope. The type checker checks the step under \Gamma_0 and discards its context \Gamma_s. The initialiser ends with \mathsf{normal}.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash c_0 \dashv \Gamma_0 \qquad \Gamma_0 \vdash e : \mathsf{bool} \\ \Gamma_0 \vdash c_s \dashv \Gamma_s \qquad \Gamma_0 \vdash \{c\} \dashv \Gamma_0 \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{for}\ (c_0;\, e;\, c_s)\ \{c\} \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-For)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash c_0 \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho_0, \sigma_0 \\ \rho_0, \sigma_0 \vdash \mathtt{while}\ (e)\ \{\, \{c\}\ c_s \,\} \Rightarrow r, \rho_0, \sigma_1 \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{for}\ (c_0;\, e;\, c_s)\ \{c\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_1 \setminus \mathrm{fresh}(\rho, \rho_0)}\;\textsf{(For)}

Braces are mandatory, and each branch is a block. An if without else has an empty block as second branch. The evaluator computes the condition first, and only the chosen branch runs.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash e : \mathsf{bool} \qquad \Gamma \vdash \{c_1\} \dashv \Gamma \\ \Gamma \vdash \{c_2\} \dashv \Gamma \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{if}\ (e)\ \{c_1\}\ \mathtt{else}\ \{c_2\} \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-If)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_e) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true} \qquad \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash \{c_1\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_2}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{if}\ (e)\ \{c_1\}\ \mathtt{else}\ \{c_2\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(If-T)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_e) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false} \qquad \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash \{c_2\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_2}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{if}\ (e)\ \{c_1\}\ \mathtt{else}\ \{c_2\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(If-F)}

The sequence carries the environment from one command to the next. A \mathsf{ret} interrupts the sequence, and the commands after it do not run.

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \varepsilon \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-Seq-Empty)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash c \dashv \Gamma_1 \qquad \Gamma_1 \vdash cs \dashv \Gamma_2}{\Gamma \vdash c\ cs \dashv \Gamma_2}\;\textsf{(T-Seq)}

\dfrac{}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \varepsilon \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma}\;\textsf{(Seq-Empty)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash c \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \rho_1, \sigma_1 \vdash cs \Rightarrow r, \rho_2, \sigma_2}{\rho, \sigma \vdash c\ cs \Rightarrow r, \rho_2, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Seq)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash c \Rightarrow \mathsf{ret}\,r, \rho_1, \sigma_1}{\rho, \sigma \vdash c\ cs \Rightarrow \mathsf{ret}\,r, \rho_1, \sigma_1}\;\textsf{(Seq-Ret)}

The rule While-T recurs on its own conclusion. A return in the body interrupts the loop, rule While-Ret. The divergence of while (true) {} has no derivation, a limitation of inductive big step semantics (Kahn, RR-0601, §4.3, p. 11).

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \mathsf{bool} \qquad \Gamma \vdash \{c\} \dashv \Gamma}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{while}\ (e)\ \{c\} \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-While)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_e) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{while}\ (e)\ \{c\} \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma_1}\;\textsf{(While-F)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_e) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true} \qquad \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash \{c\} \Rightarrow \mathsf{normal}, \rho, \sigma_2 \\ \rho, \sigma_2 \vdash \mathtt{while}\ (e)\ \{c\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_3 \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{while}\ (e)\ \{c\} \Rightarrow r, \rho, \sigma_3}\;\textsf{(While-T)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r_e, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_e) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true} \qquad \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash \{c\} \Rightarrow \mathsf{ret}\,r, \rho, \sigma_2}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{while}\ (e)\ \{c\} \Rightarrow \mathsf{ret}\,r, \rho, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(While-Ret)}

C++17 admits several base classes for one class, which g++ accepts in class C : public A, public B.

Core C++ admits one public base class, and the parser rejects a second one, Definition 6.1.1. Methods are defined inside the class.

The restriction makes the bases of a class one chain, a list from the class to its root. The order of the fields, the constructors from the root down and the destructors from the class of the object up all follow that list, Definition 6.2.1. A method call selects the method nearest the class in the list, so no member name is ambiguous between two bases, Definition 6.3.2.

In C++17 an automatic object without an initialiser has an indeterminate value. An evaluation that produces it has undefined behaviour, with some exceptions (N4659 §11.6 ¶12). A program may also declare variables outside every function. The program int main() { int x; x = 1; return x; } compiles with g++.

Core C++ requires an initialiser in every local declaration, by the grammar, Definition 4.1.1. It has no global variables. The parser rejects the program above and every declaration of a variable outside a function.

The restriction gives every location a value from its allocation, so the store never holds an indeterminate value. The environment of a function body binds only its parameters, Definition 5.1.1, and the store holds no location before main runs.

In C++17 a lambda may capture by reference. The call of its closure after the end of the lifetime of a captured entity is likely to have undefined behaviour (N4659 §8.1.5.2 ¶16). Each lambda also has a unique, unnamed closure type (N4659 §8.1.5.1 ¶1), which auto may hold.

Core C++ admits only the capture [=], and the closure holds copies of the captured values, Definition 5.3.2. A captured int or bool is a copy that the body reads and never writes. A lambda occurs only as the argument of new std::function<F>(λ), Definition 8.2.2. The parser rejects [&] and auto f = [=]() -> int { return 1; };, and g++ accepts both.

The restriction keeps the locations of the enclosing block out of every closure, so a closure never reads a freed variable. A captured pointer still reaches its object in the store, and its dereference after a delete is error. The type of every lambda is the function type F of its std::function, so the type checker needs no closure types, Definition 5.3.1.

In C++17 an object may live in a variable, and a class without a declared copy constructor gets one implicitly (N4659 §15.8.1 ¶6). The destructor of an automatic object runs implicitly when its block exits (N4659 §15.4 ¶12). So g++ accepts C c = *p;, which copies the object.

Core C++ creates every object with new and reaches it by pointer or by reference. It never copies an object, and it rejects C c = *p; with the message that objects live behind pointers. A destructor runs only on delete, Definition 6.3.4. There are no copy constructors, no RAII and no initialiser lists.

The restriction leaves no copy and no destruction at block exit. Every constructor runs on a new, and every destructor runs on a delete of the program. The rules New of Definition 6.2.1 and Delete of Definition 6.3.4 show it in the derivation. An object is one record in the store, so two names of an object hold the same location. The exit of a block frees only the locations its declarations allocated, Definition 4.4.2.

In C++17 the evaluations of the operands of an operator are unsequenced, except where the standard notes otherwise (N4659 §4.6 ¶17). The initialisations of the parameters of a call are indeterminately sequenced with respect to each other (N4659 §8.2.2 ¶5). A side effect on a memory location has undefined behaviour when it is unsequenced relative to another access to that location (N4659 §4.6 ¶17).

Core C++ evaluates left to right wherever C++17 leaves the order open, Definition 4.7.1. It keeps the orders C++17 fixes, such as the right operand before the left one in an assignment (N4659 §8.18 ¶1).

The restriction makes the order of the premises of each rule part of the rule. The store of one premise is the input of the next, so the effects of a construct happen in one order. With the mutually exclusive premises of the rules, a construct has one result, Theorem 5.6.2.

Core C++ leaves out exceptions, function templates, partial specialisation, objects by value, copy constructors, RAII, multiple inheritance, arrays and separate compilation.

Arrays violate the type completeness principle of Watt, "No operation should be arbitrarily restricted in the types of its operands" (2004, §2.5.3, p. 43). Watt counts assignment, argument passing and function results among the operations a language should not restrict. Arrays of C are not first class values in his account (§11.3, p. 270), and arrays of C++17 carry the same restrictions. An array is not assignable. A parameter of array type is adjusted to a pointer (N4659 §11.3.5 ¶5), and no function returns an array (N4659 §11.3.5 ¶10). An array converts to a pointer to its first element (N4659 §7.2). The subscript a[i] is *(a + i) (N4659 §8.2.1 ¶1), and an index outside the array is undefined (N4659 §8.7 ¶4). The library type std::vector takes the place of arrays, Definition 8.2.1. A program creates a vector with new, as any object, and an index outside the vector has no derivation.

Without exceptions, the control result of a command is normal or ret v, Definition 2.1.8. No program catches error. Without separate compilation, a program is one translation unit that the type checker sees whole. The preprocessor of Core C++ is a language of its own that runs before the compiler, Definition 1.4.1.

Each syntactic class has a relation and a function of the evaluator. The expressions have Eval and expr, and the commands Exec and cmd. The relation states the cases of its class with a result. The function covers every case of the same class, and its result is that of the relation or an error.

The rules exclude each undefined case of C++ by a premise. The rule Div requires a divisor other than zero, and Arith and Div require a result in the range of int. The rule Delete requires an object at ℓ, and a virtual destructor when the static class differs from the class of the object. When one of these premises fails, the subject has no derivation. The function of the same class then gives the cause of error that names the premise, divisionByZero, overflow, doubleDelete or deleteWithoutVirtualDtor.

The function returns into the monad CoreCpp.M, the exception transformer ExceptT Error over a state monad. The state holds only the trace of the derivation, not the store σ. Every handler of an exception in the evaluator records the trace and throws the exception again. So an error of a premise is the result of the conclusion. That monad states the propagation of error once, and no rule repeats it. The causes of error are the constructors of one type, so every case outside the rules has a name.

Two kinds of cause stay outside the pattern. The causes undeclaredVariable, undeclaredFunction, arity, typeError and notCallable arise only in a program that skipped the type checker. The cause outOfFuel marks a derivation deeper than the fuel, and it is not a result of the semantics. The agreement between each relation and its function has no Lean proof, and issue #6 records the check.

C++17 has function templates, class templates with several parameters, partial specialisation and the ranking of implicit conversion sequences in overload resolution (N4659 §16.3.3.2). The call g(true) with the overloads g(int) and g(long) selects g(int) in g++, by the promotion of bool.

Core C++ admits class templates with one type parameter, instantiated in type position, Definition 7.3.1. Overloading selects by argument type without a ranking, Definition 7.1.2. The keyword auto declares local variables only, Definition 7.4.2.

The restriction expands every template before the type check, Definition 7.3.2, so the type checker and the evaluator see only classes. The choice of an overload has three outcomes, the one candidate that accepts the arguments, an exact candidate among several, or an error.

In C++17 the branch of an if and the body of a loop may be a single statement without braces. An else then belongs to the nearest if without an else (N4659 §9.4.1 ¶1, footnote 90).

Core C++ requires braces around every branch and every body, so if (x == 0) x = 1; is a syntax error, Definition 4.5.1.

With mandatory braces the grammar of Core C++ is LL(1), a theorem checked in Lean, Theorem 1.2.2. The parser is recursive descent, with one function per nonterminal. A brace closes every branch, so no else needs a disambiguation rule.

C++17 has five standard signed integer types, and int has the natural size of the architecture (N4659 §6.9.1 ¶2). A bool converts to an int by an integral promotion (N4659 §7.6 ¶6), so g++ accepts int x = true;.

Core C++ has the basic types int, bool and void. An int is 32 bit two's complement, and its overflow is error, Definition 2.1.3. The relation \mathsf{Compat} is the identity on the basic types, so Core C++ rejects int x = true;, Definition 2.1.11.

The restriction fixes the meaning of every arithmetic operation independently of the machine. It also removes every conversion between basic types. So the choice of an overload needs no ranking of conversion sequences, Definition 7.1.2.

C++17 defines undefined behaviour as behaviour for which the standard imposes no requirements (N4659 §3.27). An expression whose result is not mathematically defined or not representable in its type has undefined behaviour (N4659 §8 ¶4). So does a zero divisor (N4659 §8.6 ¶4). So does a delete through a pointer to a base without a virtual destructor (N4659 §8.3.5 ¶3). The end of the storage duration of an object makes every pointer to it invalid. Indirection through an invalid pointer and its deallocation by a second delete have undefined behaviour (N4659 §6.7 ¶4).

Core C++ admits none of these cases, since a premise excludes each one, Definition 9.1.1. The evaluator reports error with the exit code 134, Definition 2.1.9.

The restriction gives every well typed program one of three outcomes, a value, error, or no termination. The semantics fixes the outcome, and no compiler chooses it. The examples of the repository show the difference, through bin/compare.
