A non terminating program has no derivation either. This is a limitation of the inductive big step style, not a restriction of the subset (Kahn, RR-0601, §4.4, p. 11).

Every construct has rules with mutually exclusive premises, and a Core C++ program has at most one result. The evaluation order fixed left to right removes the choice C++17 leaves to the compiler. The relations of Definition 2.2.1 make the statement precise. Two derivations of \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' for the same e give the same r and \sigma'. The same holds for Exec, Execs and the auxiliary dynamic relations. The proof in CoreCpp/Semantics/Determinism.lean is one mutual structural recursion on the first derivation. Each case either applies the rule of the second derivation or contradicts one of its premises.

The classes of the program form the class table, a finite map from class names to declarations. A declaration has an optional base, fields and methods with their visibility, at most one constructor and at most one destructor.

The table gives, for a class, its chain up to the root base, every field of the chain with the class that declares it, the nearest method of a given name, the overload set of a method name, one method per signature, the subclass relation and whether some class of the chain has a virtual destructor.

The type checker consults it for types, visibility and dispatch, and new and delete for the fields to allocate and to free. A name carries the qualification of its namespace, N::C.

The value of a lambda is the closure \mathsf{closure}(x_1 \ldots x_k, \tau, c, [y_1 \mapsto w_1, \ldots, y_m \mapsto w_m]), with the parameters, the result type, the body and the captured copies, one value per variable of the body, other than a parameter, that the environment binds.

A std::function object of Definition 8.2.2 holds a closure in its one location, as the target of the object, or \mathsf{null} for the function with no target. No variable, field or element holds a closure directly, since a std::function is an object, reached by pointer or by reference. The type of a lambda is the function type \tau(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k), which Ty.isFn recognises, and it occurs only as the template argument of std::function.

The control result of a command is \mathsf{normal} or \mathsf{ret}\,r, with r the result of the operand of return. A \mathsf{ret} interrupts sequence, block and loop up to the call that consumes it. A call whose body ends with \mathsf{normal} gives \mathsf{void} when the result type is void, and error otherwise.

The environment \rho is a finite map from identifiers to locations, and the most recent binding prevails.

Each binding records whether the declaration that made it allocated the location, as τ x = e does, or aliased an existing one, as the reference τ& y = e does. The notation \rho[x \mapsto \ell] extends \rho with an owned binding, Env.extend, and \rho[x \mapsto_{\mathsf{a}} \ell] with an alias binding, Env.alias. The set \mathrm{fresh}(\rho, \rho'), Env.fresh, holds the locations of the owned bindings of \rho' that \rho does not have. Scope exit frees these locations at the end of a block, of a for loop and of a call, so an alias never frees the location it names.

Inside a member body, this is an alias binding to the location of the receiver, made by the call and never freed by the return.

The result error is not a value of the language. In the relations it is the absence of a derivation. Whatever C++17 leaves undefined fails a premise of every rule that could reach it, \sigma(\ell) = v, n_2 \neq 0, n \in [-2^{31}, 2^{31}-1], 0 \le i < n, and the subject has no derivation, with nothing to propagate. The evaluator, which runs the relations, reports the case as error, with a message and the exit code 134, and the error replaces the result of the whole program.

Its causes are division by zero, int overflow, the dereference of nullptr, an index outside a vector, a negative vector size, a failed assert, the call of a std::function with no target, a location outside \sigma, a missing return in a non void function, a second delete of the same object, a delete through a pointer to a base class without a virtual destructor, and the exhaustion of the fuel of the evaluator, a bound on the depth of a derivation that a program without termination reaches. The causes undeclaredVariable, undeclaredFunction, arity, typeError and notCallable guard the evaluator against a program that skipped the type checker.

The function environment is the program p seen as a finite map from a name to the overload set of the functions of that name, funsNamed, and to the declarations of the library, libDecls. The program is a parameter of every relation, which reads it and never changes it. The evaluator selects a function by the signature the type checker wrote into the call, lookupSig, and the static relation by pickFun. The syntax of the declarations it holds is in Definition 1.3.1.

The type int has 32 bits in two's complement. Every rule that gives an integer has the premise n \in [-2^{31},\, 2^{31}-1], the test Int32.inRange, so a result outside the range has no derivation. The function \mathsf{int32} of the evaluator returns the integer when it lies in the range and error otherwise.

C++17 fixes neither the width nor the representation of int. A plain int has the natural size suggested by the architecture of the execution environment, with a range of at least [-32767, 32767] (N4659 §6.9.1 paragraph 2 and §21.3.5, N1570 §5.2.4.2.1). Its representation may be two's complement, ones' complement or signed magnitude (N4659 §6.9.1 paragraph 7). The range of int is therefore a property of the platform.

The ABI of the platform fixes it. The System V AMD64 psABI and AAPCS64 both give int 32 bits, and GCC supports only two's complement integer types.

An arithmetic result outside the range of int has undefined behaviour (N4659 §8 paragraph 4), and Core C++ makes it error. That boundary has to coincide with the one of g++ and clang on x86‑64 and ARM64, the implementations Core C++ follows. A wider range would give a value where C++ gives none, and a narrower one would give error where C++ gives a value.

The representation enters only through the lower bound -2^{31}. Core C++ has no bitwise operators, no shifts and no unsigned types, so no program observes a bit pattern. The width lives in Int32.min and Int32.max, and in the largest integer literal the lexer of Definition 1.1.3 accepts.

\dfrac{n \in [-2^{31},\, 2^{31}-1]}{\mathsf{int32}\,n = \mathsf{int}\,n}

A location \ell is a natural number. The store keeps a counter of the next free location. Allocation takes the counter and increments it, and the removal of a location never decreases it, so locations are never reused.

The result r of an expression is \mathsf{val}\,v or \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, after the value categories of C++17. A glvalue is an expression whose evaluation determines the identity of an object, and a prvalue is one whose evaluation computes a value (N4659 §6.10 paragraph 1). An lvalue yields the location of the object it designates, \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, and every other expression yields its value, \mathsf{val}\,v. The tag keeps the location of an object apart from a pointer value. The variable p yields \mathsf{lval}\,\rho(p) and new C() yields \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{loc}\,\ell).

The conversion \mathrm{rd}(\sigma, r) gives the value of a result. A glvalue in a context where a prvalue is expected is converted to a prvalue (N4659 §6.10 paragraph 3), and the lvalue‑to‑rvalue conversion reads the object (N4659 §7.1 paragraph 1). A location outside the store has no value, so a rule with the premise \mathrm{rd}(\sigma, r) = v has no derivation there and the evaluator gives error.

\mathrm{rd}(\sigma, \mathsf{val}\,v) = v \qquad\qquad \dfrac{\ell \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma}{\mathrm{rd}(\sigma, \mathsf{lval}\,\ell) = \sigma(\ell)}

The rules apply rd where C++17 converts. These are the operands of the operators, the conditions, the right side of an assignment, an initialiser of a variable, a by value argument, the operand of *, -> and delete, and the index of []. The left side of an assignment, the initialiser of a reference, a reference argument and the receiver of e.m(…) and e.f require \mathsf{lval}\,\ell. The expression of e; is discarded with no conversion (N4659 §8 paragraph 12). The operand of return passes its result unchanged, and the call converts it by the declared return type of the callee, Definition 5.1.1.

The store \sigma is a finite map from locations to values, with a counter of the next location. The operation \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma, v) returns the location of the counter, \ell \notin \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma, and the store \sigma[\ell \mapsto v] with the counter advanced, and allocMany allocates one location per value, in order. The operation \sigma \setminus L removes the locations of L from the domain and leaves the counter, so a freed location is never allocated again. A rule that reads or writes a location has the premise \ell \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma, so an access outside the domain has no derivation, and the evaluator gives error.

The typing context \Gamma is a finite map from identifiers to types. The types are \mathsf{int}, \mathsf{bool}, \mathsf{void}, a class C, a pointer \tau*, an instance L\langle\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k\rangle of a class template of the library, a function type \tau(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k) as template argument, and the internal type \mathsf{nullptr\_t} of nullptr.

Class types and the types of the library whose module gives new a signature, std::vector and std::function, are object types, IsObject. They have no values, and no variable, by value parameter, result or field has one, Storable. A reference parameter and a local reference may have an object type, Bindable. An expression of object type, such as *p, never stands where a value is expected, HasValues. It occurs as the left operand of ., as the operand of [] or of an operator member, as the callee of (*f)(ē), as the argument of a reference parameter and as the initialiser of a local reference.

\begin{array}{lcl} \mathsf{IsObject}(\tau) & \iff & \tau = C \ \lor\ (\tau = L\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle \land \exists\, \bar{\tau}', \tau'.\ \Gamma \vdash_L \mathtt{new}\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle : \bar{\tau}' \to \tau') \\ \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau) & \iff & \tau \neq \mathsf{void} \land \lnot\,\mathsf{IsObject}(\tau) \\ \mathsf{Storable}(\tau) & \iff & \lnot\,\mathsf{IsObject}(\tau) \land \tau \neq \mathsf{nullptr\_t} \land \tau \neq \tau'(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k) \\ \mathsf{Bindable}_{r}(\tau) & \iff & (r \land \mathsf{IsObject}(\tau)) \lor \mathsf{Storable}(\tau) \end{array}

The judgment \Gamma \vdash_L \mathtt{new}\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle : \bar{\tau}' \to \tau' is the signature that the module of L gives to the creation of an instance of L\langle\bar{\tau}\rangle, Definition 8.1.1, the relation StaticModule.new. The flag r of \mathsf{Bindable}_{r} is true for a reference.

Each binding carries a mark, read only or not. The check of a lambda body sets the mark on every binding of the enclosing scope, so that the body reads the copies of [=] and never writes them. The binding of this gives the current class, TEnv.self, inside a member body.

The judgment \Gamma \vdash \tau\ \mathsf{ok} states that the type \tau is well formed. The program declares every class it names, C \in \mathrm{dom}\,p. A header declares every type of the library it names, with its number of template arguments, L/k \in \mathrm{lib}(p), Program.libDecls, and the module of L accepts the arguments, \mathrm{wf}_L(\bar{\tau}). A function type has a storable or void result and storable parameters. The judgment does not depend on \Gamma.

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{int}\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Int)}

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{bool}\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Bool)}

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{void}\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Void)}

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathsf{nullptr\_t}\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Null)}

\dfrac{C \in \mathrm{dom}\,p}{\Gamma \vdash C\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Class)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash \tau\ \mathsf{ok}}{\Gamma \vdash \tau*\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Ptr)}

\dfrac{L/k \in \mathrm{lib}(p) \qquad \mathrm{wf}_L(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k) \qquad \Gamma \vdash \tau_i\ \mathsf{ok}}{\Gamma \vdash L\langle\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k\rangle\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Lib)}

\dfrac{\tau = \mathsf{void} \lor \mathsf{Storable}(\tau) \qquad \Gamma \vdash \tau\ \mathsf{ok} \qquad \mathsf{Storable}(\tau_i) \qquad \Gamma \vdash \tau_i\ \mathsf{ok}}{\Gamma \vdash \tau(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k)\ \mathsf{ok}}\;\textsf{(WF-Fn)}

The relation \mathsf{Compat}(\tau, \tau') states that a value of type \tau is accepted where \tau' is expected. It holds of equal types, of nullptr and a pointer type in either order, and of a pointer to a class and a pointer to one of its bases. The relation D \sqsubseteq B, Program.subclass, holds when D = B or D derives from B. These are the only implicit conversions of Core C++.

\dfrac{}{\mathsf{Compat}(\tau, \tau)}\;\textsf{(C-Refl)}

\dfrac{}{\mathsf{Compat}(\mathsf{nullptr\_t}, \tau*)}\;\textsf{(C-Null)}

\dfrac{}{\mathsf{Compat}(\tau*, \mathsf{nullptr\_t})}\;\textsf{(C-NullR)}

\dfrac{D \sqsubseteq B}{\mathsf{Compat}(D*, B*)}\;\textsf{(C-Sub)}

The relation is directional. Its left side is the type of an expression and its right side the type its context requires. The judgment \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau of Definition 5.3.1 uses it for an initialiser, the right side of an assignment, an argument and a returned value. The rule T-Eq of Definition 3.4.2 tries it in both directions, and the join of the conditional in Definition 3.5.1 chooses its type with it.

The rule C-Null is the null pointer conversion of C++ (N4659 §7.11 paragraph 1), so Node* p = nullptr;, p = nullptr; and return nullptr; type check. No declared type is \mathsf{nullptr\_t}, so every nullptr ends up converted to a pointer type. The rule C-Sub lets a pointer to a derived class stand where a pointer to its base is expected, and never the converse, since Core C++ has no cast.

Compatibility and subsumption are two relations. Subsumption D \sqsubseteq B is a relation on classes, the subclass order of the program, reflexive and transitive. It extends to types, \tau' \sqsubseteq \tau when \tau' = \tau or when both are classes in that order, Typing.refCompat. It says that an object of class \tau' is also an object of class \tau. It therefore applies where the semantics binds or chooses a location, the initialiser of a reference in Definition 4.2.1 and the branches of a conditional that denotes a location in Definition 3.5.1. No value moves there, and the object keeps its class. Compatibility \mathsf{Compat}(\tau, \tau') is a relation on the types of values. It says that a value of type \tau may stand where the context expects a value of type \tau'. It contains subsumption only through pointers, by C-Sub, since a class type has no values, and it adds the conversions of nullptr that subsumption knows nothing of.

The relation \mathsf{Compat} is not an equivalence. It is not symmetric, since \mathsf{Compat}(D*, B*) holds for a proper base B and \mathsf{Compat}(B*, D*) does not. It is not transitive either, since \mathsf{Compat}(C*, \mathsf{nullptr\_t}) and \mathsf{Compat}(\mathsf{nullptr\_t}, D*) hold for two unrelated classes C and D while \mathsf{Compat}(C*, D*) does not. The rule C-NullR causes this, and Core C++ keeps it. Without C-NullR the relation would be a preorder.

The values are \mathsf{int}\,n, \mathsf{bool}\,b, \mathsf{void}, the pointer \mathsf{loc}\,\ell, the value \mathsf{null} of nullptr, the object \mathsf{obj}\,C\,[f_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, f_n \mapsto \ell_n], a record of one location per field with its class tag, and the instance \mathsf{lib}\,L\,[\ell_0, \ldots, \ell_{n-1}] of an object type L of the library, such as a vector, with one location per element, Definition 8.2.1.

The value \mathsf{void} is the result of a call to a function without return value. The closure is a value too, Definition 2.1.6.

The tag of an object is the class that new names when it creates the object. Its fields are those of the whole chain of classes, the root base first. The tag decides the dispatch of virtual methods and the destructors that delete runs. Objects and instances of object types of the library live in the store at their own location, and a program reaches them only through pointers and references.

The default value of a type, which new gives to every field and to every element of a vector, is \mathsf{int}\,0, \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false} or \mathsf{null}.

Once a call inside an expression may write the store, the order of evaluation of the operands is part of the meaning. Core C++ fixes one order for every construction, and each rule states it by the order of its premises, the store of one premise being the input of the next.

  • In the arithmetic and relational operators, the left operand before the right one, rules Arith, Div and Rel.

  • In a call, the arguments left to right, rule Call of Definition 5.1.1 through the relation Bind.

  • In the assignment, the right side before the left one, rule Assign.

  • In the indexing of a vector, the receiver before the index, rule Index of Definition 8.1.2, which gives the location of the element.

The first two are choices of Core C++ where C++17 fixes no order. The last two are the orders C++17 fixes, for the assignment (N4659 §8.18 paragraph 1) and for the subscript (N4659 §8.2.1 paragraph 1), which an overloaded operator[] keeps (N4659 §16.3.1.2 paragraph 2). For f() + g() with effects, C++17 also admits the evaluation of g() first, and Core C++ has no such derivation, because Arith has one order of premises. The example call_order.cpp returns 21 in Core C++, and 21 or 12 under a C++ compiler.

The arithmetic operators require int on both operands. The evaluator computes the left operand before the right one, the order Core C++ chooses where C++17 fixes none. Division and remainder truncate toward zero, as in C++. A zero divisor and a result outside the range of int fail a premise, so the expression has no derivation and the evaluator gives error.

The quotient of -2^{31} by -1 is 2^{31}, outside the range, so it has no derivation. C++17 leaves the remainder undefined whenever it leaves the quotient undefined (N4659 §8.6 paragraph 4). The remainder therefore exists only when the quotient is in the range, and the remainder of -2^{31} by -1 has no derivation either.

A left operand of class type calls a member operator⊕ instead, rule T-OpBin of Definition 7.2.1.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \mathsf{int} \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \mathsf{int}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1 \oplus e_2 : \mathsf{int}}\;\textsf{(T-Arith)}, \quad \oplus \in \{+, -, *, /, \%\}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{int}\,n_1 \\ \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r_2, \sigma_2 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_2, r_2) = \mathsf{int}\,n_2 \\ n_1 \oplus n_2 \in [-2^{31},\, 2^{31}-1] \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \oplus e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{int}(n_1 \oplus n_2)), \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Arith)}, \quad \oplus \in \{+, -, *\}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{int}\,n_1 \\ \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r_2, \sigma_2 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_2, r_2) = \mathsf{int}\,n_2 \\ n_2 \neq 0 \qquad n = n_1 \oslash n_2 \qquad n,\ n_1 / n_2 \in [-2^{31},\, 2^{31}-1] \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \oslash e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{int}\,n), \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Div)}, \quad \oslash \in \{/, \%\}

In the code, the case binop of Eval.expr evaluates both operands and calls Eval.binop.

The condition is bool. For a value, both branches have types with values, neither void nor an object type, and the type of the conditional is their join, Ty.join. The join is \tau_2 when the two types are equal or when \tau_2 is a pointer type and \tau_3 is \mathsf{nullptr\_t}, \tau_3 when \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_2, \tau_3), and \tau_2 when \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_3, \tau_2). A pointer to a derived class and a pointer to its base thus join at the base. A pointer and nullptr join at the pointer type in either order, so c ? p : nullptr and c ? nullptr : p both have the type of p, the composite pointer type of C++ (N4659 §8.16 paragraph 7). The evaluator computes the condition and then only the chosen branch, whose result the conditional passes on unchanged.

The predicates \mathsf{HasValues} and \mathsf{IsObject} are those of Definition 2.1.10.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash e_1 : \mathsf{bool} \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \tau_2 \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_3 : \tau_3 \\ \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau_2) \qquad \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau_3) \qquad \tau = \mathrm{join}(\tau_2, \tau_3) \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1\ ?\ e_2 : e_3 \;:\; \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Cond)}

\mathrm{join}(\tau_2, \tau_3) = \begin{cases} \tau_2 & \text{if } \tau_2 = \tau_3 \text{ or } \tau_2 = \tau'* \text{ and } \tau_3 = \mathsf{nullptr\_t} \\ \tau_3 & \text{else if } \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_2, \tau_3) \\ \tau_2 & \text{else if } \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_3, \tau_2) \end{cases}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true} \qquad \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r, \sigma_2}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1\ ?\ e_2 : e_3 \Rightarrow r, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Cond-T)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false} \qquad \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_3 \Rightarrow r, \sigma_2}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1\ ?\ e_2 : e_3 \Rightarrow r, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Cond-F)}

When the two branches are lvalues of one type, the conditional is an lvalue and yields the location of the chosen branch (N4659 §8.16 paragraph 5). The rules Cond-T and Cond-F give that location, since they pass on the result of the branch. So (c ? x : y) = 7 assigns to x or to y, and int& r = c ? x : y; binds a reference. The access (c ? *p : *q).value reaches a field without copying an object. Branches of object type must denote locations, rule T-CondObj, so c ? *p : *q never copies. The two types must be equal, or a class and one of its bases, which join at the base, Typing.locJoin. The program then reaches the derived object as an object of its base, as C++ binds it (N4659 §8.16 paragraph 4). A call of a virtual method dispatches on the class of the chosen object, and a member of the derived class alone is a type error.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \mathsf{bool} \qquad \Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e_2 : \tau_2 \qquad \Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e_3 : \tau_3 \qquad \tau = \mathrm{locJoin}(\tau_2, \tau_3)}{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e_1\ ?\ e_2 : e_3 \;:\; \tau}\;\textsf{(T-LocCond)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e_1\ ?\ e_2 : e_3 \;:\; \tau \qquad \mathsf{IsObject}(\tau)}{\Gamma \vdash e_1\ ?\ e_2 : e_3 \;:\; \tau}\;\textsf{(T-CondObj)}

The dereference *e is an lvalue. It yields the location the value of e holds, with the store the evaluation of e leaves. When the pointer is \mathsf{null} the premise of Deref fails, so there is no derivation and the evaluator gives error, where C++17 leaves the dereference undefined. A pointer after delete holds a location outside the store, and the conversion rd of Definition 2.1.7 has no derivation there.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \tau*}{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} {*e} : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-LocDeref)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma', r) = \mathsf{loc}\,\ell}{\rho, \sigma \vdash {*e} \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(Deref)}

The field access e.f is an lvalue. It yields the location of the field f in the record at the location e yields. The access e->f yields the field of the record its pointer holds, as (*e).f does, so a null pointer has no derivation and the evaluator gives error. The record must be in the store, so an access through a pointer after delete has no derivation either. The premise C \text{ has } \tau\, f holds of a field of C or of one of its bases, and a private field must be visible from \Gamma, Program.visibleField and Definition 6.1.2.

The equation \mathrm{field}_{\Gamma}(C, f) = \tau states that C or one of its bases declares the field \tau\, f and that f is visible from \Gamma, Program.visibleField.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : C \qquad \mathrm{field}_{\Gamma}(C, f) = \tau}{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e.f : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-LocField)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : C* \qquad \mathrm{field}_{\Gamma}(C, f) = \tau}{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e\mathtt{->}f : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-LocArrow)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, \sigma' \qquad \sigma'(\ell) = \mathsf{obj}\,C\,[\ldots f \mapsto \ell_f \ldots]}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e.f \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell_f, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(Field)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma', r) = \mathsf{loc}\,\ell \qquad \sigma'(\ell) = \mathsf{obj}\,C\,[\ldots f \mapsto \ell_f \ldots]}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e\mathtt{->}f \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell_f, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(Arrow)}

An integer literal has type int and a boolean literal has type bool. Evaluation leaves the store unchanged. The rule Lit has the range premise of Definition 2.1.3, which never fails, because the lexer of Definition 1.1.3 rejects a literal above 2^{31}-1.

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash n : \mathsf{int}}\;\textsf{(T-Lit)}

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash b : \mathsf{bool}}\;\textsf{(T-BoolLit)}

\dfrac{n \in [-2^{31},\, 2^{31}-1]}{\rho, \sigma \vdash n \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{int}\,n), \sigma}\;\textsf{(Lit)}

\dfrac{}{\rho, \sigma \vdash b \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{bool}\,b), \sigma}\;\textsf{(BoolLit)}

Conjunction and disjunction require bool and short circuit. The evaluator computes the second operand only when the first one does not decide the result. A class never overloads them.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \mathsf{bool} \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \mathsf{bool}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1 \odot e_2 : \mathsf{bool}}\;\textsf{(T-Logic)}, \quad \odot \in \{\&\&, ||\}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \mathbin{\&\&} e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false}), \sigma_1}\;\textsf{(And-False)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true} \\ \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r_2, \sigma_2 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_2, r_2) = v \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \mathbin{\&\&} e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}\,v, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(And-True)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \mathbin{||} e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{true}), \sigma_1}\;\textsf{(Or-True)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = \mathsf{bool}\,\mathtt{false} \\ \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r_2, \sigma_2 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_2, r_2) = v \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \mathbin{||} e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}\,v, \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Or-False)}

In the code, the cases binop .and and binop .or of Eval.expr implement the two pairs of rules.

A variable is an lvalue. It yields the location the environment assigns to it, and the store does not change. A variable that a lambda captures by copy is read only in \Gamma, so it denotes no location for the type checker, and no assignment reaches it. Inside a member body an unqualified field of this is an lvalue too, rule VarField of Definition 6.1.3, with the typing rule T-LocVarField. The other lvalues, *e, e.f and e->f, are the nodes of the last section. An element v[i] of a vector is a use of the library, Definition 8.1.2.

The set \mathrm{const}(\Gamma) holds the variables of \Gamma captured by copy inside a lambda, TEnv.isConst.

\dfrac{\Gamma(x) = \tau \qquad x \notin \mathrm{const}(\Gamma)}{\Gamma \vdash_{\ell} x : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-LocVar)}

\dfrac{\rho(x) = \ell}{\rho, \sigma \vdash x \Rightarrow \mathsf{lval}\,\ell, \sigma}\;\textsf{(Var)}

The expression new C() allocates one location per field of C and of its bases, each with the default value of its type, Ty.default, then the record itself, tagged with the class. The constructors of the chain then run on the record, from the root base down, and the expression evaluates to a pointer to the record. Its type is C*. A class without a constructor takes no arguments, so the empty parentheses are its whole argument list. The typing rule below is the one of a class without constructor. The evaluation rule is the case without arguments, in which a constructor of a base runs with none. A class with a constructor takes its arguments in the parentheses, Definition 6.2.1.

The program p maps a class C to its declaration \mathit{cd}, Program.lookupClass, whose constructor \mathit{cd}.\mathrm{ctor} is \bot when it has none. The premise C \in \mathrm{dom}\,p states that p declares C, a nonempty Program.chain. The list \mathrm{fields}(C) holds the fields of C and of its bases, the root base first, Program.allFields. The judgment \rho, \sigma \vdash \mathrm{ctors}(\ell, C) \Rightarrow \sigma' runs the constructors of the chain of C on the object at \ell, from the root base down, each with \mathtt{this} \mapsto \ell, the relation Ctors.

\dfrac{p(C) = \mathit{cd} \qquad \mathit{cd}.\mathrm{ctor} = \bot}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{new}\ C() : C*}\;\textsf{(T-New)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} C \in \mathrm{dom}\,p \qquad \mathrm{fields}(C) = [\tau_1\, f_1, \ldots, \tau_n\, f_n] \\ (\ell_i, \sigma_i) = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma_{i-1}, \mathrm{default}\,\tau_i),\ \sigma_0 = \sigma \\ (\ell, \sigma') = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma_n, \mathsf{obj}\,C\,[f_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, f_n \mapsto \ell_n]) \\ \rho, \sigma' \vdash \mathrm{ctors}(\ell, C) \Rightarrow \sigma'' \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{new}\ C() \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{loc}\,\ell), \sigma''}\;\textsf{(New)}

The literal nullptr has the internal type \mathsf{nullptr\_t}, compatible with itself and with every pointer type, and with no other. Its value is \mathsf{null}.

\dfrac{}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{nullptr} : \mathsf{nullptr\_t}}\;\textsf{(T-Null)}

\dfrac{}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{nullptr} \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}\,\mathsf{null}, \sigma}\;\textsf{(Null)}

The value of *e, e.f, e->f or e[i] is the content of the location it yields, the conversion rd of Definition 2.1.7, applied by the context that requires a value. No evaluation rule of its own reads it. A location outside the store has no value, and the evaluator gives error. Three typing rules give the value the type of the location. The element v[i] of a vector takes its location from the library, rule Index of Definition 8.1.2.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \tau*}{\Gamma \vdash {*e} : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Deref)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : C \qquad \mathrm{field}_{\Gamma}(C, f) = \tau}{\Gamma \vdash e.f : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Field)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : C* \qquad \mathrm{field}_{\Gamma}(C, f) = \tau}{\Gamma \vdash e\mathtt{->}f : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Arrow)}

Equality compares two int, two bool, two pointers, or nullptr with a pointer or with nullptr, when \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_1, \tau_2) or \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_2, \tau_1), the test Ty.comparable. A pointer to a derived class thus compares with a pointer to its base, Definition 6.3.1. Two pointers are equal when they are the same location, and nullptr equals only nullptr. Order compares two int, and there is no order on pointers. The result is bool, and the evaluator computes the left operand before the right one. A left operand of class type calls a member operator, as in Definition 3.4.1.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma \vdash e_1 : \tau_1 \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \tau_2 \qquad \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_1, \tau_2) \lor \mathsf{Compat}(\tau_2, \tau_1) \\ \tau_1, \tau_2 \in \{\mathsf{int}, \mathsf{bool}, \tau*, \mathsf{nullptr\_t}\} \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1 \bowtie e_2 : \mathsf{bool}}\;\textsf{(T-Eq)}, \quad \bowtie \in \{==, \mathrel{!=}\}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e_1 : \mathsf{int} \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_2 : \mathsf{int}}{\Gamma \vdash e_1 \bowtie e_2 : \mathsf{bool}}\;\textsf{(T-Rel)}, \quad \bowtie \in \{<, <=, >, >=\}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \Rightarrow r_1, \sigma_1 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_1, r_1) = v_1 \\ \rho, \sigma_1 \vdash e_2 \Rightarrow r_2, \sigma_2 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_2, r_2) = v_2 \qquad v_1 \bowtie v_2 = b \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e_1 \bowtie e_2 \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{bool}\,b), \sigma_2}\;\textsf{(Rel)}, \quad \bowtie \in \{==, \mathrel{!=}, <, <=, >, >=\}

Logical negation requires bool and arithmetic negation requires int. Negation has the range premise, because the negation of -2^{31} overflows, and that negation has no derivation.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \mathsf{bool}}{\Gamma \vdash\, !e : \mathsf{bool}}\;\textsf{(T-Not)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \mathsf{int}}{\Gamma \vdash -e : \mathsf{int}}\;\textsf{(T-Neg)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma', r) = \mathsf{bool}\,b}{\rho, \sigma \vdash\, !e \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{bool}\,\neg b), \sigma'}\;\textsf{(Not)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma', r) = \mathsf{int}\,n \qquad -n \in [-2^{31},\, 2^{31}-1]}{\rho, \sigma \vdash -e \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}(\mathsf{int}(-n)), \sigma'}\;\textsf{(Neg)}

In the code, the case unop of Eval.expr evaluates the operand and calls Eval.unop, which applies Eval.int32 to -n.

The value of x is \mathrm{rd}(\sigma, \mathsf{lval}\,\rho(x)) = \sigma(\rho(x)), which the context reads where it requires a value, Definition 2.1.7. The premise \ell \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma of rd fails for a location that left the store, so that read has no derivation and the evaluator gives error. Inside a member body x may be a field of this, rule T-VarField of Definition 6.1.3, and the location then comes from VarField.

\dfrac{\Gamma(x) = \tau}{\Gamma \vdash x : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Var)}

The search doubles an upper bound from 1 until the program does not exhaust it, capped at b, and then halves the interval between the last exhausted fuel and that bound. Both phases keep two invariants. The lower end exhausts the fuel and the upper end does not. Fuel 0 exhausts it, since every function of the evaluator gives outOfFuel with fuel 0. The binary search stops at an interval (d - 1, d]. By Theorem 2.4.4, a fuel that exhausts the evaluator makes every smaller fuel exhaust it too, so every j \le d - 1 exhausts it.
Let p pass prepare and run p b eq outOfFuel. The search leastFuel p b gives the least fuel d with run p d eq outOfFuel. So d \le b, run p d eq outOfFuel, and run p j = outOfFuel for every j < d.

A lambda has no type of its own. The judgment \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau, e is acceptable at \tau, checks a lambda against the function type expected where it occurs, the argument of new std::function<F>(λ) in Definition 8.2.2. For any other expression it is \Gamma \vdash e : \tau' with \mathsf{Compat}(\tau', \tau).

The type checker checks the body under \Gamma with every variable of the enclosing scope marked read only, the copies of [=]. The parameters of the lambda are ordinary variables, and the result type of the body is the result type \tau of the lambda.

The rule T-LocVar requires a variable that is not read only, so an assignment to a captured variable, or a reference to it, is a type error.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \tau' \qquad \mathsf{Compat}(\tau', \tau) \qquad \tau' \text{ has values}}{\Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau}\;\textsf{(Accept)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \Gamma' = \Gamma \text{ marked read only}, [x_1 \mapsto \tau_1, \ldots, x_k \mapsto \tau_k]\qquad \Gamma' \vdash c \dashv \Gamma'' \text{ with result type } \tau \\ \tau = \mathsf{void} \lor \mathsf{Storable}(\tau) \qquad \mathsf{Storable}(\tau_i) \qquad \tau, \tau_i \text{ well formed} \end{array}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{[=]}(\tau_1\,x_1, \ldots, \tau_k\,x_k)\ \mathtt{->}\ \tau\ \{c\} \lhd \tau(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k)}\;\textsf{(T-Lambda)}

Anywhere else a lambda is a syntax error, since the grammar admits it only as an argument of new. As the argument of a new of a class of the program it is a type error, since no constructor parameter has a function type. The grammar chapter, Definition 1.3.3, explains the decision.

Let f \mapsto \tau\ f(\tau_1\,x_1, \ldots, \tau_k\,x_k)\ \{c\} be in the program. The environment of the function holds only the parameters, because there are no global variables.

Each argument is checked at the type of its parameter by the judgment \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau of Definition 5.3.1, so that a lambda may be an argument. A variable f of a std::function type in \Gamma hides the function named f, and the call is then Definition 5.3.3.

\dfrac{f \notin \Gamma \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_i \lhd \tau_i \quad (1 \le i \le k)}{\Gamma \vdash f(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-Call)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} f \notin \rho \qquad \rho, \sigma'_{i-1} \vdash e_i \Rightarrow r_i, \sigma_i \quad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_i, r_i) = v_i \quad (\ell_i, \sigma'_i) = \mathrm{alloc}(\sigma_i, v_i) \quad (1 \le i \le k,\ \sigma'_0 = \sigma) \\ \rho_f = [x_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, x_k \mapsto \ell_k] \qquad \rho_f, \sigma'_k \vdash c \Rightarrow \kappa, \rho', \sigma'' \qquad \mathsf{Returns}(\sigma'', \kappa, \tau, r) \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash f(e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow r, \sigma'' \setminus (\{\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_k\} \cup \mathrm{fresh}(\rho_f, \rho'))}\;\textsf{(Call)}

The control of the body is \kappa. The return frees the copies of the arguments and the locals the body declared, \mathrm{fresh}(\rho_f, \rho') of Definition 2.1.4. After a call the store holds only what existed before it and the objects created with new.

The predicate \mathsf{Returns}(\sigma, \kappa, \tau, r) gives the result r of a call whose body ends with the control \kappa in the store \sigma, for a callee declared with the result type \tau. The operand of return initialises the result of the call by the declared return type (N4659 §9.6.3 paragraph 2). For a callee declared \tau the result is the value of the operand, read in \sigma before the locals leave the store, the order of N4659 §9.6.3 paragraph 3. For a method declared \tau\& the result is the location of the operand, rule Returns-Ref of Definition 7.2.2. A body that ends with \mathsf{normal} gives \mathsf{void} if \tau = \mathsf{void}, and otherwise there is no derivation. A missing return in a non void function is an error of the evaluator, not a type error. C++17 leaves it undefined in a function other than main (N4659 §9.6.3 paragraph 2). For main the rule departs from C++17, where the end of main is a return 0 (N4659 §6.6.1 paragraph 5).

\dfrac{\mathrm{rd}(\sigma, r) = v}{\mathsf{Returns}(\sigma, \mathsf{ret}\,r, \tau, \mathsf{val}\,v)}\;\textsf{(Returns-Ret)}

\dfrac{}{\mathsf{Returns}(\sigma, \mathsf{normal}, \mathsf{void}, \mathsf{val}\,\mathsf{void})}\;\textsf{(Returns-Void)}

The rule above is the case in which every parameter is by value, and Definition 5.2.1 gives the case of a parameter by reference.

A call through a function object, (*f)(e₁, …, eₖ) for a pointer f, evaluates the callee to the object and reads its target, a closure. It then evaluates the arguments by value and left to right, and allocates fresh locations for the captured copies and for the parameters. The body runs in an environment with those bindings only, and the return frees them with the locals of the body.

When the callee is a reference g to a function object, g(…) is this rule and not the call of the function named g.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \mathtt{std{:}{:}function}\langle\tau(\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_k)\rangle \qquad \Gamma \vdash e_i \lhd \tau_i \quad (1 \le i \le k)}{\Gamma \vdash e(e_1, \ldots, e_k) : \tau}\;\textsf{(T-CallFn)}

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma_0 \qquad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_0, r) = \mathsf{lib}\ \mathtt{std{:}{:}function}\,[\ell_t] \qquad \sigma_0(\ell_t) = w \\ \rho, \sigma_{i-1} \vdash e_i \Rightarrow r_i, \sigma_i \quad \mathrm{rd}(\sigma_i, r_i) = v_i \quad (1 \le i \le k)\qquad \mathrm{apply}(\sigma_k, w, (v_1, \ldots, v_k)) \Rightarrow v, \sigma' \end{array}}{\rho, \sigma \vdash e(e_1, \ldots, e_k) \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}\,v, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(CallFn)}

The target w is a closure, and the function with no target, \mathsf{null} at \ell_t, has no derivation, so its call is error in the evaluator. The application of the closure to the values is a judgment of its own. It allocates the captured copies and then the arguments, allocMany of Definition 2.1.5, and its body ends as the body of Definition 5.1.1 does.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} v = \mathsf{closure}(x_1 \ldots x_k, \tau, c, [y_1 \mapsto w_1, \ldots, y_m \mapsto w_m]) \\ (\ell'_1 \ldots \ell'_m\, \ell_1 \ldots \ell_k, \sigma_1) = \mathrm{allocMany}(\sigma, w_1 \ldots w_m\, v_1 \ldots v_k) \\ \rho_c = [y_1 \mapsto \ell'_1, \ldots, y_m \mapsto \ell'_m, x_1 \mapsto \ell_1, \ldots, x_k \mapsto \ell_k] \\ \rho_c, \sigma_1 \vdash c \Rightarrow \kappa, \rho'', \sigma'' \qquad \mathsf{Returns}(\sigma'', \kappa, \tau, \mathsf{val}\,v') \end{array}}{\mathrm{apply}(\sigma, v, (v_1, \ldots, v_k)) \Rightarrow v', \sigma'' \setminus (\{\ell'_1, \ldots, \ell'_m, \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_k\} \cup \mathrm{fresh}(\rho_c, \rho''))}\;\textsf{(Apply)}

A function is well typed when its body is well typed under the context of its parameters and its result type. Its result type is void or storable, each parameter type is bindable, and every type is well formed. A reference parameter may thus have an object type.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \tau = \mathsf{void} \lor \mathsf{Storable}(\tau) \qquad \mathsf{Bindable}_{r_i}(\tau_i) \qquad \tau, \tau_i \text{ well formed} \\ [x_1 \mapsto \tau_1, \ldots, x_k \mapsto \tau_k] \vdash c \dashv \Gamma' \text{ with result type } \tau \end{array}}{\vdash \tau\ f(\tau_1\,x_1, \ldots, \tau_k\,x_k)\ \{c\}}\;\textsf{(T-Fun)}

The return yields the control \mathsf{ret}\,r, with the result r of its operand unchanged, a location when the operand is an lvalue. Seq-Ret and While-Ret propagate it up to the call, which converts it by the declared return type, \mathsf{Returns} of Definition 5.1.1. The program keeps the form return e that C++17 prescribes, and no rewrite of the operand takes place. The expression of return e is acceptable at the result type \tau_r of the enclosing body.

\dfrac{\tau_r = \mathsf{void}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{return} \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-RetVoid)}

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau_r \qquad \tau_r \neq \mathsf{void}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{return}\ e \dashv \Gamma}\;\textsf{(T-Ret)}

\dfrac{}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{return} \Rightarrow \mathsf{ret}(\mathsf{val}\,\mathsf{void}), \rho, \sigma}\;\textsf{(ReturnVoid)}

\dfrac{\rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma'}{\rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{return}\ e \Rightarrow \mathsf{ret}\,r, \rho, \sigma'}\;\textsf{(Return)}

The abstract syntax is the tree form of the grammar of Definition 1.2.1, with one inductive type or structure per class of nonterminals. It has no parentheses and no precedence, because the tree fixes the structure. The table below gives the alternatives of every constructor of Syntax.lean, in the order of the file, with the constructor in the right column.

The type Ty has the basic types int, bool and void, class types, pointer types, the types of the library such as std::vector<int>, function types, and \mathsf{nullptr\_t}, the internal type of nullptr.

The type UnOp has ! and unary -, and the type BinOp has the arithmetic, the comparison and the logical operators.

The type Expr has literals and variables, operators and the conditional, and three calls, of a named function, of a method and of the std::function an expression denotes, as in (*f)(ē). It has the two forms of new, this, field access through . and ->, dereference and indexing, and the lambda.

The type Cmd has the block, if, while, for and return, the declarations with a type, with a reference and with auto, the assignment, the expression statement and delete.

A Param may be by reference. A Fun has a return type, a name, parameters and a body. A Vis is public or private.

A member is a Field, a Method, a Ctor or a Dtor. A method also records whether it is virtual, whether it overrides and whether it returns a reference, and a destructor records whether it is virtual. A ClassDecl has a qualified name, an optional base, fields and methods with their visibility, at most one constructor and at most one destructor.

A Decl is a class, a function, a class template, or a class template or a function of the library declared without a body. A Program is a list of declarations.

The symbols on the left are the nonterminals of this grammar, each named after the type of Syntax.lean it describes. The nonterminal Member stands for the four structures Field, Method, Ctor and Dtor.

The rules of the typing and of the evaluation abbreviate them, τ for a Ty, e for an Expr, c for a Cmd and p for a Param, and a subscript tells two occurrences apart.

Inside the productions, n stands for an integer literal and b for a boolean one, x for a variable, f for a field or a function and m for a method, all of them written as a VarId, and C for a class, B for a base, T for a template parameter and L for a library class, all of them written as a TypeId.

The right column names, for each alternative, the constructor of the inductive type of Syntax.lean that the alternative builds, Expr.intLit for a literal and Cmd.block for a block. The type is written out on the first line of a category and only the constructor afterwards.

A constructor here is a case of an inductive definition of Lean, and not the member of a class that new runs, which this table calls Ctor.

Every field and every method carries a Vis, which the parser takes from the section that holds it. The constructor and the destructor are public and carry no visibility.

The grammar of Core C++, in EBNF. The superscript X^{*} repeats X zero or more times, and the superscript X^{?} makes X optional. Large parentheses group, the bar separates alternatives, and terminals are in typewriter font. The grammar has no left recursive production, and it is left factored.

A statement is a command or an expression followed by ;. Assignment is a command, and ExprStatement joins the two forms that start with an expression to keep the grammar LL(1).

In the abstract syntax the commands form the type Cmd, and the expression statement is the command exprStmt, which evaluates and discards the value. The left side of an assignment must denote a location, a check made by the type checker.

A lambda expression is a NewArg and not a Primary, so it occurs only as an argument of new. The reason is the status of std::function. The header <functional> declares it as a class template, as C++ does, and every class type of Core C++ is an object type, created with new, reached by pointer or reference and never held by value, so a lambda has no position of its own. A declaration std::function<F> f = λ; or a return λ; would hold the object by value, which the subset excludes, and no library rule enters the grammar of declarations or of return. The grammar reads token classes and cannot name std::function, so it stops at the argument of new, and the type checker narrows the position to new std::function<F>(λ), the one type that expects a function type, by Definition 5.3.1. Writing the lambda in new std::function<F>(λ) keeps every Core C++ program a C++17 program.

The parser rejects forms that the grammar derives and the subset excludes.

A class template with a body has one type parameter, and an instantiation of a class template of the program has one template argument. A class of the library always takes template arguments, and a base class is a class of the program.

A lambda parameter is by value, and a field is not a reference. A namespace holds only classes, templates and namespaces.

Only a header of Core C++ opens the namespace std, declares a function without a body or declares a class template without a body, since C++ leaves a program that adds declarations to std undefined (N4659 §20.5.4.2.1, paragraph 1). Preproc marks the lines that come from a header, and the parser reads the marks. The type checker then rejects a class template or a function without a body that no module of the library implements.

The parser also checks the names of the constructor and the destructor against their class. A class has at most one of each, both are public, and a field is never virtual. The public destructor is a restriction of the subset, since C++ accepts a private destructor that no code outside the class calls.

The proof is a computation. The theorem CoreCpp.Grammar.isLL1_grammar builds the predictive parsing table of the grammar of Definition 1.2.1 and checks that no entry holds two productions.

The grammar comes from the file grammar/core-cpp.ebnf, rule by rule over token classes. The generator lake exe ebnf2lean reads the file, maps its terminals to the token classes by ofEbnf and writes the rules as the module CoreCpp/GrammarRules.lean by leanModule, and the theorem is about the rules of that module.

The library LL1 of the package ll1-lean translates them from EBNF to BNF. It then computes the nullable nonterminals, FIRST and FOLLOW as least fixed points, and fills the table.

Three left factorings and one restriction of the language explain the result.

In Member, a TypeId opens both a constructor and the type of a field or method. The next token decides, ( for a constructor and any other token for a type.

In ExprStatement, an assignment and an expression statement share the prefix Expr, and the token = decides.

In Declaration, a class template with a body and a class template of the library without one share the prefix up to class. The case of the name decides, a TypeId for the first and a VarId for the second.

In Statement, the FIRST sets of LocalDecl and ExprStatement are disjoint. A local declaration starts with auto, int, bool, void, a TypeId or an NsId. An expression starts with a VarId, an IntLit, true, false, nullptr, this, new, (, !, - or *, and never with a TypeId or an NsId.

The restriction shapes Chain. After a . or a ->, an argument list opens the arguments of a method, so e.f(a) and e->f(a) are method calls and never the call of a function held in a field. The nonterminal After says exactly that, since a field access continues through ChainNoCall, which no argument list may follow directly.

Without the restriction the two readings would both derive e->f(a) and no lookahead would separate them.

A field holds a pointer to a function object and the call goes through it, as in (*b->handler)(3), and b->handler(3) is a type error that names the field.

The same table drives the nonrecursive predictive parser LL1.Grammar.parse, which CoreCpp.Grammar.derive runs on the tokens of a program without the end token, each mapped to its class by Term.ofToken, and whose output is the leftmost derivation. The function parseTree builds the derivation tree from that derivation.
The grammar is LL(1).

Type inference in Core C++ is local. The rule of auto is T-Auto of Definition 4.1.1, and it covers pointers to instantiations, since a pointer has values.

\dfrac{\Gamma \vdash e : \tau \qquad \mathsf{HasValues}(\tau) \qquad \mathsf{Storable}(\tau)}{\Gamma \vdash \mathtt{auto}\ x = e \dashv \Gamma[x \mapsto \tau]}\;\textsf{(T-Auto)}

A lambda has no type of its own, so it never initialises an auto, which the grammar already guarantees. Core C++ has no inference over a whole program, such as the type inference of Hindley (Trans. AMS 146, 1969, pp. 29–60, doi:10.1090/S0002-9947-1969-0253905-6) and Milner (JCSS 17, 1978, pp. 348–375, doi:10.1016/0022-0000(78)90014-4).

The proof is one mutual structural recursion on the derivation, in CoreCpp/Semantics/InterpComplete.lean. The predicate Done c a states that the computation c gives a from every state. A rule whose premises the functions reach with fuels n_i is reached with fuel 1 + \sum n_i, or 2 + \sum n_i where a premise is the method lookup or the field lookup, and with any larger fuel. The loops of Call, Member, New and Delete follow the derivations of Bind, Ctors and Dtors one element at a time. The relations of the library give a value of the function of their module.

The proof exposed one divergence of the relation from CallLib. The rule requires that f is no function of the program, and the relation required only that no function named f has the chosen signature. A program with a function and a header declaration of one name thus had a derivation that the evaluator did not reach. The relation now requires p.funsNamed f = [], as T-CallLib does.

A derivation in a relation of the dynamic semantics is reached by the function of its judgement with enough fuel. A derivation of \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' gives a fuel n such that expr with any fuel m \ge n gives (r, \sigma') on \rho, \sigma and e, from every state of the monad M. The same holds for cmd, cmds and the auxiliary functions. In particular p \Rightarrow v implies runMain p m = ok v for every m from some bound on. Radix states it for its commands as Stmt.interp_complete, with one fuel.
Let p \Rightarrow v. By Theorem 2.4.6, runMain p m = ok v for every m from some bound k on. By Theorem 2.4.4, runMain p (max n k) is runMain p n, which is error e. The two results differ.

An error of the evaluator other than outOfFuel means that the program has no result. If runMain p n = error e with e \neq outOfFuel, then p \Rightarrow v has no derivation for any v. Radix has no counterpart.

The proof is by induction on n, for all the functions of the evaluator at once, in CoreCpp/Semantics/FuelMono.lean. The relation LeP compares two runs, and its congruence lemmas cover sequencing, the caught errors, traced, tracedLib, tracedCases, the conditional and the loops of for. With fuel 0 every function gives outOfFuel, and the statement holds vacuously. With fuel n + 1 and m + 1 the two bodies coincide except for the fuel of the recursive calls, where the induction hypothesis applies. A run that does not end in outOfFuel has no recursive call that ends in it, because every error that a body catches, in traced and in the cases of tracedCases, the body throws again. The theorem of Radix, Stmt.interp_fuel_mono, covers the successful results only. This one covers the errors too, which the search for the least fuel of Theorem 2.4.8 needs.

Let n \le m. A result of a function of the evaluator with fuel n that is not the error outOfFuel is its result with fuel m, from the same arguments and the same state of the monad M. The value or the error, the trace and the state after the run coincide. In particular run p n \neq outOfFuel implies run p m = run p n.

The proof is by induction on n, for all the functions of the evaluator at once, in CoreCpp/Semantics/InterpSound.lean. The predicate Ok c P states that every value of the computation c satisfies P. Its lemmas cover sequencing, the caught errors, traced, tracedLib, tracedCases and the loops of for. Each case of a function builds the rule its comment names from the induction hypothesis on the premises. The loops of Call and Member build Bind from the last parameter back, and the loops of applyVals give the allocations of Apply. A function of CoreCpp.Std gives a derivation in the relation of its module. The evaluator collects the owned locations in reverse order, and \sigma \setminus L depends only on the elements of L.

The proof exposed one divergence of the evaluator from CallLib. The rule requires (f, k) in libDecls for a call with k arguments, and the evaluator checked the name alone. A header that declared assert with two parameters thus let assert(true) give a value with no derivation. The evaluator now checks the arity and gives the guard arity otherwise.

A value of a function of the evaluator has a derivation in the relation of its judgement, for every fuel and every state of the monad M. A value (r, \sigma') of expr on \rho, \sigma and e gives a derivation of \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma'. The same holds for cmd, cmds and the auxiliary functions. In particular runMain p n = ok v implies p \Rightarrow v. The statement holds for every program, well typed or not. Radix states it for its commands as Stmt.interp_sound.

The judgment \rho, \sigma \vdash c \Rightarrow r, \rho', \sigma' states that the command c yields the control r, the environment \rho' and the store \sigma'. The output environment exists so that a declaration extends \rho for the following commands, and the block discards the extension and frees its owned locations when it ends.

The judgment \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' states that the expression e, under the environment \rho and the store \sigma, has the result r and yields \sigma'. The result is \mathsf{lval}\,\ell for an lvalue, the location of the object it designates, and \mathsf{val}\,v for any other expression, Definition 2.1.7. The lvalues are a variable, an unqualified field of this, a dereferenced pointer, a field of an object, a field through a pointer, a call of a member that returns a reference, an element of a vector, and a conditional whose chosen branch is one. The store enters expressions because a call or a new inside an expression may change it.

One judgment serves both the value and the location of an expression, as in the L‑values and R‑values of Strachey (1967, reprinted in Higher‑Order and Symbolic Computation 13, 2000). The context decides, by the conversion rd of Definition 2.1.7.

The semantics is a set of inductive propositions, one per judgment, with one constructor per rule. A constructor bears the name of its rule in this blueprint. The relations of the language are in CoreCpp/Semantics/Static.lean and Dynamic.lean, and the relations of the modules of the library in Library.lean. A constructor follows the layout of a rule on the board, the premises one per line, the inference line with the name, and the conclusion under it. The program p is a parameter of every relation, the function table and the class table.

The judgments \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau and \Gamma \vdash c \dashv \Gamma' differ in subject and in output. Acceptance judges an expression at a type its context expects, so \tau is an input. It extends \Gamma \vdash e : \tau by the compatibility of types and by lambdas. The judgment on commands judges a command under the result type \tau_r of the enclosing body. Its output is the context \Gamma' the command extends \Gamma to, as a declaration does.

Lean writes the configuration \langle\rho, \sigma\rangle in angle brackets, and \langle\Gamma, \tau_r\rangle for a command with the result type of its body. A sequence takes a starred arrow. Both are concessions to the parser of Lean. The relation is the specification and the function its interpreter. Every recursive function of the type checker and of the evaluator takes as first argument the fuel, a bound on the depth of a derivation, and recurses on it. The constant typingFuel and the function runWith set it to 10^6, and its exhaustion is the error outOfFuel. The fuel makes two theorems expressible, soundness, that a result of the function is a derivation of the relation, and completeness, that the function reaches every derivation with enough fuel. Both hold, Theorem 2.4.5 and Theorem 2.4.6. A larger fuel keeps every result that does not exhaust it, Theorem 2.4.4. The structure follows Radix, the language of the tutorial of de Moura at ETAPS 2026, and the theorems take the names of their counterparts in Radix.

The judgments on declarations, \vdash f, \vdash C and \vdash p, are structures of named conditions rather than relations with one constructor. Their conditions are side conditions on the declarations and not premises on subterms. The selection of an overload, Definition 7.1.2, is the work of the type checker, which writes its choice into the call, and the relation reads it.

The evaluator runs in the monad M, which carries the trace of the derivation. When tracing is on, each rule application records the instance of the rule it concludes, or the error, at its depth in the tree, with the antecedent and the consequent in parts. The trace records a premise of the library under the rule of its module, such as V-New, the creation of a vector in Definition 8.2.1, or F-New, the creation of a function object in Definition 8.2.2. The state survives the error, so the trace keeps the rule applications up to the failing rule. The log holds the instances in post order, each premise before its conclusion.

The function renderTrace rebuilds the tree from the log. It lays the tree out as a derivation on the board, the premises over a line of inference, the conclusion under it and the rule name at the right.

A legend names the environments \rho_i, the stores \sigma_j and the subjects longer than 40 characters, so every judgment fits one line. The function writes a subtree wider than 100 columns apart, under a name \mathcal{D}_k.

The judgment \Gamma \vdash c \dashv \Gamma' states that the command c is well typed and extends \Gamma to \Gamma', so that a declaration reaches the following commands of the sequence. Kahn writes the output of a declaration after a colon, \rho_1 \vdash \mathrm{DECL} : \rho_2 (RR-0601, §2.3). Core C++ writes \dashv instead, because the colon already introduces a type in \Gamma \vdash e : \tau, and \dashv marks an output context, as in Dunfield and Krishnaswami (2013). The result type \tau_r of the enclosing body, a function, a member or a lambda, is a parameter of the relation, written \langle\Gamma, \tau_r\rangle in Lean.

The judgment \Gamma \vdash e : \tau states that the expression e has type \tau in the context \Gamma. Each rule concludes about one constructor of Expr, and a constructor may have several rules, as the call of a name has four. T-Call calls a function of the program, Definition 5.1.1. T-CallFn calls a function object that a variable names, Definition 5.3.3. T-CallThis calls a method of the receiver inside a member body, Definition 6.1.3. T-CallLib calls a function a header declares, Definition 8.1.2. A lambda has no rule of this judgment. The judgment \Gamma \vdash e \lhd \tau accepts it at its function type, and accepts any other expression by its type.

A static judgment that fails gives a type error, and the type checker stops at the first one.

The judgment \Gamma \vdash_{\ell} e : \tau holds for the expressions that denote a location, a variable not captured by copy, an unqualified field of this, *e, e.f, e->f, the element e[i] of a vector, an operator[] or a method call whose member returns a reference, and a conditional whose two branches denote locations of one type.

A lambda evaluates to a closure with copies of the variables of its body that the environment binds, its parameters excluded, at the evaluation of the lambda. The closure holds values, not locations. A captured int or bool is a copy the body reads and never writes. A captured pointer still reaches its object in \sigma, so an effect through it is visible outside the lambda.

\dfrac{\begin{array}{c} \{y_1, \ldots, y_m\} = \text{variables of } c \text{ bound in } \rho, \text{ minus the } x_i\qquad \rho(y_j) = \ell_j \\ \ell_j \in \mathrm{dom}\,\sigma\qquad w_j = \sigma(\ell_j) \end{array}}{\begin{array}{c} \rho, \sigma \vdash \mathtt{[=]}(\tau_1\,x_1, \ldots, \tau_k\,x_k)\ \mathtt{->}\ \tau\ \{c\} \\ \Rightarrow \mathsf{val}\,\mathsf{closure}(\vec{x}, \tau, c, [y_1 \mapsto w_1, \ldots, y_m \mapsto w_m]), \sigma \end{array}}\;\textsf{(Lambda)}

The function lex maps a string to an array of tokens ended by eof. It runs the automaton Lexer.run and then the pass of Definition 1.1.2. It discards white space and line comments, reads the longest run of digits as an integer literal, the longest run of identifier characters as an identifier, and tries the symbols of three, two and one characters in that order. Any other character is a lexical error.

The lexer also rejects what C++ would read otherwise, so that every Core C++ program is a C++ program with the same meaning.

  • It rejects a keyword of C++ or an alternative representation such as and outside the reserved words of the subset (N4659 §5.11, Tables 5 and 6).

  • It rejects an integer literal of two or more digits with a leading 0, which C++ reads in octal, and one above 2147483647, to which C++ gives a type wider than int.

  • It reads -- and ++ as tokens that no production uses, so 5--2 fails as in C++, where the longest match gives --.

The automaton Lexer.run is partial, so Lean records an opaque constant that carries the type and not the body, and no property of it is proved here.

The function identifier first looks an identifier up in the reserved words and then classifies it by its initial. A further pass over the token array, qualifiers, marks as an NsId every identifier whose next token is ::, of either case.

The pass runs after the automaton, so it sees neither white space nor comments and marks std :: vector as it marks std::vector. The function parseUnit of Definition 1.3.4 runs the automaton on each line of the Preproc output alone and the pass once on the tokens of all the lines, so a :: that starts a line marks the identifier that ends the line before.

That class is what lets a qualified name open a type where the case convention alone would read a variable, so std::vector<int> needs no reserved word.

Tokens fall in six classes, and the end token eof closes the array.

  • Reserved words, the 24 words int, bool, void, if, else, while, for, return, true, false, auto, delete, new, nullptr, this, class, public, private, virtual, override, namespace, template, typename and operator.

  • Type identifiers, TypeId, with an uppercase initial.

  • Variable identifiers, VarId, with a lowercase initial or _, naming variables, fields, functions and methods.

  • Namespace identifiers, NsId, the identifiers of either case that :: follows.

  • Decimal integer literals, IntLit.

  • Operators and punctuation, with [=] as a single token by the longest match rule.

There is no token >>, so Stack<Stack<int>> closes with two tokens >.
